Hi genealogy enthusiasts! My brother and I both did DNA tests for fun over the holidays and just got our results back. We were comparing them tonight and some things seem really weird - can someone help us understand what we're looking at? We're both confused and wondering if maybe the lab made a mistake.

My Results:
- Irish/Scottish: 45%
- German: 23%
- Scandinavian: 18%
- Italian: 14%

My Brother's Results:
- Irish/Scottish: 46%
- German: 22%
- Eastern European: 31%
- Middle Eastern: 1%

Here's what's confusing us:

DNA Relatives section:
- We show up as "Close Family" to each other
- We share 1,847 cM (centimorgans) - not sure what this means?
- I match with cousins on "Mom's side": Karen, Susan, Michael (all 400-600 cM)
- He matches with the same cousins: Karen, Susan, Michael (same amounts)
- But on "Dad's side" it's weird:
    - I match with cousin Tommy (578 cM) and Uncle Jim's kids (390 cM each)
    - My brother shows NO matches to Tommy or Uncle Jim's kids at all
    - Instead he has matches to people with names I don't recognize

We're only 2 years apart and our parents have been married 30 years! We look so much alike that everyone says we could be twins. Is this normal? Maybe different kids inherit different sides of the family more strongly?

We were going to surprise Mom and Dad with a big family tree project for their anniversary next month. Should we contact the DNA company about what seems like missing connections?

It's great that you have taken such an interest in understanding your family history! Let's break down your results and investigate why things may look different between your DNA matches.

The percentage breakdowns you see reflect your genetic ancestry. These are rough estimates and can vary between testing companies due to differences in reference populations. The test is not a precise indicator but rather an estimate that helps you better understand your genetic heritage. It's interesting that you both share a large portion of Irish/Scottish heritage, which may reflect an ancestor who was of mixed Scottish and Irish descent or even a more recent Irish ancestor.

The centimorgans (cM) shared between you means that you share an amount of DNA expected between an average parent-child, full sibling or grandparent-grandchild pair. 1847 cM is approximately the amount of DNA you would share with a full siblings (on average). This makes sense because you are indeed full siblings.

When you look at your shared matches, it gets a little more confusing - the amounts of DNA you share with your identified cousins on the maternal side match up, which supports the idea that those are all descendants of your mother's mother or father. But the absence of shared matches on your father's side suggests that there could be some additional complexity in your paternity.

It's worth noting that full siblings, although related through both parents, can have mismatches in some of their genetic information, due to the random manner in which genetic material is divided between siblings. This appears to have happened in your situation.

Given your parents' marriage duration and your similar appearance, the discrepancy on the paternal side seems an unusual finding. It could be that there are mistakes in the paternal lineage of your family tree, recording errors, or some other issues. It would be worthwhile to dig deeper and possibly have a conversation with your parents or older relatives for more details, or contact the DNA testing company to see if any further analysis can explain the differences.

Regarding the DNA matches showing up under your brother's name that he hadn't identified before, it could be due to having grandparents or other close relatives who recently did the test and share matches with him on the distant side. Again, it is important to cross-reference the details of each match's tree and contact information provided by the DNA profile to zero in on any discrepancies.

If you proceed to gather the family tree information as planned, adding in your DNA results could potentially give further clarity or raise more interesting questions about your family history. Just remember, DNA testing isn't a replacement for family history gathering; it's a great tool to use alongside it.

Do share your findings with your father and see if it sparks any further memories or lets them clarify anything. Genealogy is a fascinating and nuanced field and it’swortheverydigitating and exploring as a family. Happy investigating!
